386.title: Passover night (Exodus 12:1–14)
386.hook: a lamb, blood on the doorposts, eaten in haste, and the angel passes over
386.howItsDone: Jewish families keep Passover each spring with the Seder meal and the retelling of the Exodus; Christians celebrate Easter as their Pascha, and Catholic and other liturgical churches read Exodus 12 on Holy Thursday, the evening they remember the Last Supper.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the plagues, and a king whose every no made the next one easier. Your line was a hard heart gets harder. Where did you pause before an automatic no? Day three hundred eighty-six.

Some meals are just meals. Others get described for years afterward: who sat where, what was said, what the room smelled like. A last dinner before someone moved away. The table the night before a wedding, or after a funeral. Exodus is about to describe a meal like that, the night before everything changes. Nine plagues have struck Egypt. One more is coming, the death of the firstborn. And before it falls, God gives Moses and Aaron instructions. Not for a battle. For dinner.
screen: `SOME MEALS YOU REMEMBER.` → `ONE PLAGUE LEFT.` → `INSTRUCTIONS FOR DINNER.`

segments.voice: Each household is to take a lamb, a young male without blemish. Keep it a few days. Then, at twilight, kill it, and put some of its blood on the two doorposts and the top of the door frame of the house. Roast it whole and eat it that night with unleavened bread and bitter herbs. And eat it dressed for travel, in the King James Bible: "with your loins girded, your shoes on your feet, and your staff in your hand; and ye shall eat it in haste: it is the LORD's passover." Shoes on. Ready to walk out the door. Then the promise: "when I see the blood, I will pass over you." That's the word. Pesach in Hebrew, Passover in English. The plague will pass over the marked houses. And then, before any of it has happened, God says this night must be remembered: "this day shall be unto you for a memorial; and ye shall keep it a feast." A feast of remembering, commanded before the event even begins. Jewish families still keep it. At the Passover Seder, children ask why this night is different from all other nights, and the story is told again at the table. Christians carry this night too. The Gospels set Jesus's last supper and his death at Passover time, and Paul writes, "Christ our passover is sacrificed for us." That is why in many languages the word for Easter comes from Pesach: Pascha. The night carries grief too. The deliverance of one people came with death in the houses of another, and the Seder remembers that: a drop of wine is taken from the cup for each plague as it is named.
screen: `A LAMB WITHOUT BLEMISH.` · `BLOOD ON THE DOORPOSTS.` · `SHOES ON, STAFF IN HAND.` · `PESACH, PASCHA, EASTER.` · then, large: `WHEN I SEE THE BLOOD, I WILL PASS OVER YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: eat something standing, remembering. Take a cracker, a piece of bread, a sip of water, whatever is near. Stand up if you can. Hold it for a moment. Think of a night in your own life that changed everything, or the story of someone who came before you and got out of something hard. Eat slowly, standing, shoes on, as if you might have to leave. If you pray, you can give thanks for deliverance. If you don't, simply remember. The bell holds the time.
Passover. Pesach in Hebrew: the night the plague passed over the houses marked with the lamb's blood, kept as a feast of remembering ever since.
Your line: remember this night. Today, tell someone younger one story from your family's past that they've never heard. Day three hundred eighty-six.

fork.setup: you're an Israelite father in Egypt. Moses says: kill a lamb, mark your doorposts with its blood, and eat it tonight dressed to travel. what do you do?

fork.reveal: the people do as they are told. "when I see the blood, I will pass over you." the night is to be remembered forever.

original.note: Hebrew: Passover, from the verb to pass over or spare. the root of the Greek Pascha.

trapdoor: what you thought: Passover is a Jewish holiday that comes around Easter.
what it means: a meal eaten in haste on the night of deliverance, commanded to be remembered forever, and kept by Jews to this day.

what a scholar hears: Pesach became Greek Pascha, which gave the word for Easter in many languages; the Gospels date Jesus's death by Passover, though John and the other Gospels place the meal on slightly different days.

387.title: Out in haste (Exodus 12:29–42)
387.hook: no time for the bread to rise; they leave that night
387.howItsDone: Jews eat matzah through the week of Passover to remember the hurried departure; Latin-rite Catholics and some Protestant churches use unleavened bread or wafers at communion, while Orthodox churches use leavened bread.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Passover: a lamb, blood on the doorposts, a meal eaten with shoes on. Your line was remember this night. Which family story did you pass on? Day three hundred eighty-seven.

A hurried leaving has a look to it. The phone charger still in the wall. The coffee warm on the counter. The half-packed bag. You take what's in your hands and you go. At midnight in Egypt, the last plague falls. In the King James Bible: "there was a great cry in Egypt; for there was not a house where there was not one dead." Pharaoh's own son among them. And in the middle of the night, the king who said no again and again sends for Moses and Aaron.
screen: `WHAT GETS LEFT BEHIND.` → `MIDNIGHT IN EGYPT.` → `A GREAT CRY.`

segments.voice: Pharaoh says: "Rise up, and get you forth from among my people." Go. Take your flocks. Take everything. And then, from Pharaoh himself: and bless me also. The Egyptians push them out, urging them to hurry. There's no time to finish anything. And Exodus records the detail that people still taste every year: "the people took their dough before it was leavened, their kneadingtroughs being bound up in their clothes upon their shoulders." The bread hadn't risen. So they bake it flat on the road, unleavened cakes, because they were thrust out and could not wait. That flat bread, matzah, is what Jews eat at Passover to this day. It's the taste of leaving before you were ready. Two more details are easy to miss. First: "a mixed multitude went up also with them." Not only Israelites. Others went out with them, and the text doesn't say who they were. Second, the text stops and counts: four hundred and thirty years in Egypt, and on the very day they ended, the people went out. Then it says the night itself belongs to God: "It is a night to be much observed unto the LORD." A night God kept watch over, so Israel keeps watch on it every year. Christians carry the bread forward too. Latin-rite Catholics and some Protestant churches use unleavened bread or wafers at communion, recalling the Passover setting of the Last Supper. Orthodox churches use leavened bread, which Orthodox writers explain as a sign of the risen life. Same table, different loaves.
screen: `RISE UP, AND GET YOU FORTH.` · `DOUGH BEFORE IT WAS LEAVENED.` · `A MIXED MULTITUDE WENT TOO.` · `A NIGHT TO BE MUCH OBSERVED.` · then, large: `UNLEAVENED, IN A HURRY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: leave one thing unfinished without guilt. Settle, and breathe. Think of the list running in your head right now: emails, laundry, the project, the call. Pick one thing on it that doesn't need finishing today. Picture setting it down, like dough that didn't get to rise. Not failing. Just leaving. Notice how much of your weight is unfinished things. If you pray, you can hand that list to God for two minutes. If you don't, simply put it down. The bell holds the time.
Matzah. Hebrew for unleavened bread, made without yeast: the flat cakes Israel baked in haste, with no time for the dough to rise.
Your line: unleavened, in a hurry. Today, when you're rushing, let one imperfect thing go out the door as it is. Day three hundred eighty-seven.

trapdoor: what you thought: unleavened bread is a religious rule about yeast.
what it means: it's the taste of leaving before you were ready, carried on people's shoulders out of slavery.

what a scholar hears: Exodus 12:37–38 gives six hundred thousand men on foot plus a mixed multitude; historians debate those numbers, and Jewish and Christian readers have long discussed who the mixed multitude were.

388.title: The sea (Exodus 14:10–31)
388.hook: the sea ahead, chariots behind: stand still and see
388.howItsDone: Exodus 14 is read at the Easter Vigil in Catholic churches and others that keep the Vigil, linking the crossing of the sea to baptism, and some Christians turn to "stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD" in times of fear.

segments.voice: Yesterday, matzah: dough carried on shoulders, a mixed multitude, a night to be remembered. Your line was unleavened, in a hurry. What did you let go out the door unfinished? Day three hundred eighty-eight.

They're barely out of Egypt when Pharaoh changes his mind. Why did we let our slaves go? He takes six hundred chosen chariots and all the chariots of Egypt and chases them. The Israelites are camped by the sea. They look up and see the dust cloud coming. Water in front of them. Army behind them. No way around. And the people turn on Moses. In the King James translation: "Because there were no graves in Egypt, hast thou taken us away to die in the wilderness?" We told you to leave us alone. Slavery was better than this.
screen: `PHARAOH CHANGES HIS MIND.` → `SEA AHEAD, CHARIOTS BEHIND.` → `NO GRAVES IN EGYPT?`

segments.voice: Moses answers: "Fear ye not, stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD, which he will shew to you to day." And then: "The LORD shall fight for you, and ye shall hold your peace." Stand still. Be quiet. Watch. For frightened people, that's a hard instruction. And then, strangely, God says almost the opposite: "Wherefore criest thou unto me? speak unto the children of Israel, that they go forward." Stand still, and go forward. Both. The stillness isn't doing nothing. It's stopping the panic, so you can see the way when it opens. Moses stretches out his hand. A strong east wind blows all night and drives the sea back. And the people walk through on dry ground, "and the waters were a wall unto them on their right hand, and on their left." The Egyptians follow, the wheels come off their chariots, the water returns, and the army is lost. The Hebrew name for this water is yam suph. Older translations say Red Sea. But suph is the word Exodus uses for the reeds where baby Moses's basket was hidden, so some readers say Sea of Reeds. The text never says where it was. A later Jewish story tells of a man named Nahshon who walked into the water up to his neck before it parted. Christians have read this crossing as a picture of baptism: Paul writes that the Israelites were all "baptized unto Moses in the cloud and in the sea." Exodus fourteen is read at the Easter Vigil in Catholic churches and others that keep that night, when new Christians may be baptized. Through the water, from slavery to freedom.
screen: `FEAR YE NOT. STAND STILL.` · `SPEAK, THAT THEY GO FORWARD.` · `A WALL ON THE RIGHT AND LEFT.` · `YAM SUPH: RED SEA, OR REEDS?` · then, large: `STAND STILL, AND SEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand still for one minute. If you can, stand up. Feet flat, arms loose, eyes open or closed. Think of the thing that feels like chariots behind you right now, the worry that's chasing you. Don't run from it, and don't fight it. Just stand still. Let your breathing slow. Notice that you are here, and you are standing. If you pray, you can say Moses's words: fear not, stand still. If you don't, just stay still, and see what you notice. The bell holds the time.
The sea. The water Israel crossed on dry ground, with an army behind and a wall of water on either side.
Your line: stand still and see. Today, before you react to the next thing that panics you, stand still for three breaths, then take one step forward. Day three hundred eighty-eight.

389.title: Miriam's tambourine (Exodus 15:19–21)
389.hook: Miriam takes a tambourine and the women dance and sing
389.howItsDone: Some churches sing the Song of the Sea (Exodus 15) as a canticle at morning prayer or at the Easter Vigil, and in some Christian communities drums and dancing are part of worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sea: chariots behind, water ahead, and Moses saying stand still and see. Where did you stand still before you stepped forward? Day three hundred eighty-nine.

Here's a small question hiding in the text. When the Israelites left Egypt in the middle of the night, with dough on their shoulders and no time to pack, who brought the tambourines? Someone did. Someone, packing in the dark, made room for a drum. On the far shore, with the sea closed behind them, Moses leads the people in a long song of victory. Then the text turns to someone else. A woman we may have met before, years ago, standing in the reeds watching a basket. Now she's holding a hand drum.

In the King James Bible: "And Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a timbrel in her hand; and all the women went out after her with timbrels and with dances." A timbrel is a hand drum, a frame drum, the tof in Hebrew. And notice her title: the text calls her a prophetess. She doesn't just play. She leads, and she calls the song: "Sing ye to the LORD, for he hath triumphed gloriously; the horse and his rider hath he thrown into the sea." It's almost exactly the first line of Moses's song, turned into a call to everyone else. Moses sang, I will sing. Miriam turns it around: sing ye. Two lines, short enough for a whole crowd to pick up and shout back. Exodus doesn't name the sister by the river, but tradition says it was Miriam. If so, the girl who watched her baby brother float in the reeds is the woman who leads the dancing on the other side of the water. There is also a hard side to the song, and Jewish teachers saw it. The Talmud tells of angels in heaven wanting to sing as the Egyptians drowned, and God stopping them: the work of my hands is drowning in the sea, and you would sing? Some readers hear in that story a line between thanks for rescue and joy at someone's death. Christians sing Exodus fifteen too; some churches use it as a canticle in morning prayer. Music, it turns out, was one of the things worth carrying out of Egypt.
screen: `MIRIAM THE PROPHETESS.` · `TIMBRELS AND DANCES.` · `THE GIRL BY THE RIVER, YEARS LATER.` · `THANKS, NOT JOY AT DEATH.` · then, large: `SING YE TO THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: dance or tap a rhythm in thanks. Think of one thing you've been brought through: an illness, a bad year, a dangerous moment, a long wait that ended. Now give it a beat. Tap your hand on your knee, or the table, or your chest. Slow at first. Let it grow, the way Miriam's drum drew the women after her. Stand and sway if you like. If you pray, you can let the rhythm be your thanks to God. If you don't, let it be thanks anyway. The bell holds the time.
Miriam's tambourine. The hand drum Miriam the prophetess played on the far shore of the sea, leading the women in dance and song.
Your line: sing to the lord. Today, put on one song that lifts you, and let yourself move a little, even in the kitchen. Day three hundred eighty-nine.

what a scholar hears: Miriam's couplet repeats Moses's opening line in 15:1 almost word for word, but turns 'I will sing' into 'sing ye', a call to everyone.

390.title: Manna (Exodus 16:1–21)
390.hook: bread from heaven each morning, enough for the day, and it rots if hoarded
390.howItsDone: Christians pray "give us this day our daily bread" in the Lord's Prayer, and many read John 6, where Jesus calls himself the bread of life, alongside the manna story, especially when teaching about communion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Miriam's tambourine: a drum carried out of Egypt, and a call to sing to the Lord. Did you let yourself move to a song? Day three hundred ninety.

A month after the sea, the singing has stopped. They're in the wilderness of Sin, a stretch of desert, and the food from Egypt has run out. And memory does what memory does. The people complain to Moses and Aaron, in the King James Bible: we wish we'd died in Egypt, "when we sat by the flesh pots, and when we did eat bread to the full." Flesh pots. Pots of meat. Slavery has become, in their memory, a buffet. Anyone who has ever missed a bad job or a bad relationship because at least you knew what you were getting knows this feeling. And God's answer is not a lecture. It's breakfast.
screen: `A MONTH AFTER THE SEA.` → `THE FOOD RUNS OUT.` → `THE FLESH POTS OF EGYPT.`

segments.voice: "Behold, I will rain bread from heaven for you." In the morning, when the dew lifts, the ground is covered with something small and flaky, fine as frost. The people look at it and ask each other, in Hebrew, man hu? What is it? "It is manna: for they wist not what it was." The name is literally a question. They named their daily bread what is it. Exodus later says it tasted like wafers made with honey. And then the rules. Gather what each person needs for one day. Some gather more, some less. But when they measure it, "he that gathered much had nothing over, and he that gathered little had no lack." Everyone has enough. And don't keep any till morning. Some do anyway, just in case. By morning, "it bred worms, and stank." You can't stockpile this bread. You have to trust there'll be more tomorrow. Christians hear this story in the Lord's Prayer: give us this day our daily bread. Not this year's. Today's. Paul quotes the line about much and little when he asks one church to share with another, so that everyone has enough. And in John's Gospel, after feeding a crowd, Jesus talks about the manna and says: "I am the bread of life." Many Christians understand communion in that light. Today's word teaches something hard for people who like to plan. A few weeks ago we watched Joseph store grain for seven years, and that was wise. Here, the lesson is the other half of wisdom: some things can only be received one day at a time.
screen: `MAN HU? WHAT IS IT?` · `MUCH HAD NOTHING OVER.` · `KEPT TILL MORNING, IT STANK.` · `GIVE US THIS DAY.` · then, large: `ENOUGH FOR TODAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take only what you need today. Settle, and breathe. Think through today: the food you'll eat, the things you might buy, the time you'll spend scrolling or stocking up. Where are you gathering more than today needs, just in case? Pick one place. Picture taking only enough. Notice the small fear that comes with it, and notice it pass. If you pray, you can pray the old words: give us this day our daily bread. If you don't, simply rest in enough. The bell holds the time.
Manna. From the Hebrew question man hu, what is it? The bread from heaven that came each morning in the wilderness, enough for one day.
Your line: enough for today. Today, at one meal or one store, take only what you need, and notice what enough feels like. Day three hundred ninety.

391.title: Hold up his arms (Exodus 17:8–13)
391.hook: Moses' arms tire on the hill, and Aaron and Hur hold them up
391.howItsDone: Some Christians use the picture of Aaron and Hur holding up Moses's hands when they pray for their pastors, missionaries and one another, and some churches form prayer teams named for it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, manna, named for a question, what is it: bread that came each morning and rotted if you hoarded it. Your line was enough for today. Where did you take only enough? Day three hundred ninety-one.

Try this right now, if you can. Raise both arms over your head and hold them there. Ten seconds is easy. Thirty, your shoulders start to burn. A minute, and they begin to shake. Now imagine holding them up all day, from morning until sunset. At a place called Rephidim, a people called Amalek attack Israel. A later book says they struck at the stragglers, the tired and weak at the back of the line. Moses sends a man named Joshua to choose fighters and lead them. And Moses climbs a hill with the staff of God in his hand, and two companions, his brother Aaron, and a man named Hur.
screen: `ARMS UP: TEN SECONDS, A MINUTE.` → `AMALEK ATTACKS.` → `UP THE HILL, STAFF IN HAND.`

segments.voice: Then comes a strange battle report. In the King James translation: "when Moses held up his hand, that Israel prevailed: and when he let down his hand, Amalek prevailed." The fight down in the valley follows Moses's arms up on the hill. What did the raised hands mean? The text doesn't explain. It only shows. The Mishnah, a collection of Jewish teaching, asks it directly: did Moses's hands make the war or break it? Its answer: when Israel looked upward and turned their hearts to God, they prevailed. Christian readers have seen prayer in it too. And Moses gets tired. Of course he does. "But Moses' hands were heavy; and they took a stone, and put it under him, and he sat thereon; and Aaron and Hur stayed up his hands, the one on the one side, and the other on the other side; and his hands were steady until the going down of the sun." Look at what they do. First a stone, so he can sit. No shame in sitting. Then one on each side, holding up an arm. They don't take the staff from him. They don't do his job. They just hold up what he can't hold anymore by himself. And notice what nobody says. Nobody tells Moses to be stronger. Heavy is allowed. It's just a tired man, and friends who won't let him drop. Christians have read this as a picture of praying for one another and carrying each other, and some churches speak of holding up their pastors' arms. Joshua wins the battle down below. But the real picture is up on the hill: three people, one stone, and arms that stay up until sunset.
screen: `HANDS UP, ISRAEL PREVAILED.` · `MOSES' HANDS WERE HEAVY.` · `A STONE TO SIT ON.` · `ONE ON EACH SIDE.` · then, large: `HIS HANDS WERE STEADY UNTIL THE GOING DOWN OF THE SUN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: support someone who's tired. Settle, and breathe, and let your arms rest in your lap. Think of someone whose arms are heavy right now: a parent of small children, a caregiver, a nurse, a teacher, a pastor, a friend carrying more than their share. Picture yourself on one side of them, holding up an arm. What would that actually look like? A meal, a ride, a message, an hour of your time. Choose one. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Rephidim. The place where Amalek attacked Israel, and where Aaron and Hur held up Moses' arms until sunset.
Your line: hold up their arms. Today, do the one thing you chose for someone who's tired, and don't wait for them to ask. Day three hundred ninety-one.

what a scholar hears: the Mishnah asks whether Moses's hands made the war or broke it, and answers that Israel prevailed when they looked upward and turned their hearts to God.

392.title: Jethro's advice (Exodus 18:13–27)
392.hook: his father-in-law says: you'll wear yourself out, share the load
392.howItsDone: Some churches point to Exodus 18 when they appoint elders, deacons or lay leaders to share the work of a congregation, and some pastors cite Jethro's advice when talking about burnout and shared ministry.

segments.voice: Yesterday, at Rephidim, Moses stood on the hill with his arms getting heavy, and Aaron and Hur on either side. Your line was hold up their arms. Whose arms did you hold up? Day three hundred ninety-two, the end of week fifty-six.

A line has formed outside a tent in the desert. It started at sunrise. By noon it snakes past the cooking fires. A man wants to know whose goat it really was. Two cousins are fighting over a well. A widow has a complaint about her neighbor's fence, or the desert version of a fence. And at the front of the line, on a seat, sits one man hearing every single case himself: Moses. The people stand there, the text says, from the morning until the evening. Then an older man who has just arrived for a visit stands at the back and watches the whole day. He's Moses' father-in-law, Jethro, a priest from Midian. And when the long day is over, he says out loud what he has seen.
screen: `A LINE OUTSIDE A TENT.` → `ONE MAN HEARS EVERY CASE.` → `AN OLD MAN WATCHES ALL DAY.`

segments.voice: Here is what Jethro says, in the King James Bible: "The thing that thou doest is not good." Blunt. Then the reason: "thou art not able to perform it thyself alone." He's not saying Moses is lazy or proud. He's saying this will wear him out, and wear the people out too, standing in that line all day. Then he offers a plan. Keep the hard cases, and the work of teaching the people the way. But find able people to judge the everyday ones, over groups of a thousand, a hundred, fifty and ten. And he says what kind of people: those who fear God, who tell the truth, who hate a bribe. Moses listens. He does exactly what his father-in-law says. Notice who gave the advice. Jethro isn't an Israelite. He's a priest of Midian, an outsider, and earlier in the chapter he hears the whole story of the rescue from Egypt and blesses God for it. The Bible lets a foreign father-in-law teach the great leader something about leadership, and it doesn't seem embarrassed at all. Jewish tradition honors him in a striking way: the weekly Torah reading that contains the Ten Commandments is named Yitro, after Jethro. Christians have read this chapter in many ways. Some churches point to it when they choose elders or deacons. Others hear in it permission to ask for help. Moses, who has talked with God at a burning bush, still can't carry a whole people alone. And that's been the shape of the whole week: a night of remembering, a hurried exit, a sea, a song, manna, tired arms held up, and now the load shared.
screen: `THIS IS NOT GOOD.` · `THOU ART NOT ABLE ALONE.` · `ABLE PEOPLE OVER TENS AND FIFTIES.` · `THE ADVICE CAME FROM AN OUTSIDER.` · then, large: `THOU ART NOT ABLE TO PERFORM IT THYSELF ALONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one thing to hand over. Settle, and breathe. Picture your own line outside the tent: everything that's waiting on you this week. Let it form, one thing at a time. Now look down the line for one item somebody else could do. Not badly. Just differently than you would. A task at work. A chore at home. A worry you've been carrying for a friend who could carry it themselves. Notice what makes it hard to let go. If you pray, you can ask for the Jethro in your life to speak up. The bell holds the time.
Jethro's advice. A father-in-law from Midian watches Moses judge alone from morning to evening and says: share the load, or it will wear you out.

Your line: you can't do it alone. Today, delegate one thing, out loud, to someone who can do it, and then leave it with them. And that's week fifty-six: Passover, haste, the sea, a tambourine, manna, tired arms, and Jethro. Day three hundred ninety-two.
